After two years and a new roof, Elmbridge Library reopens its doors

Posted on 17 October 2026 by Imogen Hart

Elmbridge Library reopened on Saturday morning after a two-year restoration, with a queue of several hundred people stretching down Chapel Street before the doors opened at nine.

The Victorian building had been closed since a storm tore away part of its roof and water poured into the reference room, damaging around four thousand books and much of the original oak panelling. Insurance covered the repairs to the roof, but the town council and a local fundraising campaign paid for almost everything else.

Visitors will notice the biggest change on the first floor, where the old reference room has become a quiet reading room with long tables, green-shaded lamps and space for forty people. The ceiling, hidden for decades behind a suspended grid, has been restored to show its painted beams.

Downstairs, the children's library has doubled in size and now opens straight onto the garden at the back, which volunteers have replanted with herbs and fruit trees. There is a new room for local history, holding the town's newspaper archive back to 1871, maps and parish records that had been in storage.

"People kept asking us when they could come back, at the bus stop, in the supermarket, everywhere," said head librarian Ewan MacLeod. "A library is not only about books. It is somewhere warm and free to sit, to use a computer, to meet people. The town missed that."

The fundraising campaign, which began with a cake sale and a sponsored readathon, raised a little over 210,000 pounds from more than three thousand donors. Their names are listed on a board beside the main staircase, carved by students from the college's joinery course.

Opening hours will be longer than before the closure, with the library staying open until eight in the evening on weekdays. A programme of author talks, homework clubs and computer classes for older residents begins next month, and a full list of events is on the library's notice board.

Imogen Hart writes about arts and heritage for the Gazette. Send her your stories about local history.
